event_title: Topology seminar:  An irreducible real projective plane in the 4-sphere
combined_title: Topology seminar:  An irreducible real projective plane in the 4-sphere: Gheehyun Nahm (Princeton)
description:
Abstract: One challenge in studying knotted surfaces (surfaces embedded in 4-manifolds) is producing "genuinely new" examples. For example, until recently, every known knotted real projective plane in the 4-sphere could be expressed as the connected sum of a knotted 2-sphere and an unknotted real projective plane. Such knotted real projective planes are called reducible, or of Kinoshita type, and the Kinoshita conjecture stated that every knotted real projective plane in the 4-sphere is reducible.
I will begin by reviewing some constructions of knotted surfaces and surveying previous work on knotted real projective planes and irreducible knotted surfaces of other topological types. Then, I will present an irreducible real projective plane in the 4-sphere, which is joint work with Mark Hughes, Seungwon Kim, and Maggie Miller.

description:
Camille Ann Brewer lives and works in the City of Detroit, Michigan.  Through the process of textile construction, Brewer’s artwork intersects cartographic and photographic images that speak to specific spaces and time. Weaving together of physical place, memory with time is the core subject of this body of work.  

The artwork is built with time-period paper maps, which illustrate spatial geography and political territory; along with paper-collaged images of people, places and things, which tie directly to the history and human relationships in space.  In patterns that support the artwork’s theme, the two disparate paper elements are then woven together to create a serendipitous making and aesthetic experience.

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

combined_title: Lila Kadaj Exhibition: Tic Tic
description:
Lila Kadaj received her MFA from Wayne State University. Her work has been shown at numerous institutions, including the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Cranbrook Art Museum, and the Arab American National Museum.  She spent nearly 27 years teaching art at Detroit Public schools.

Artist statement: “When looking at a beautiful flower.  It’s just itself.  Just there......no .....it does not proclaim its purpose for blooming is to make people happy. It just is. Like standing in front of an easel and painting........just is.......no matter......what proclamations may be concluded to sway the viewer. Same thing goes for fine art.  It’s not about I am a woman....it’s not about I am a first generation Arab American.....it’s not about being a child of trauma....it’s not about a member of my family being gunned down on the street....it’s about being born a painter.....standing in front of my easel and working to create a "Piece of Fine Art". Not standing on some soap box and expecting my words to somehow qualify my painting. It’s the painting, drawing or sculpture that must speak on its own.......on how the artist......via the intellect and muse uses the elements to create something distinct and first rate.   It can be quiet or loud. I see so much very weak work uplifted not for its quality but because it’s in fashion.”

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

combined_title: Like the flowing river: An exhibition by Tomoyuki Ueno
description:
Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience.

This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor.

*The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

combined_title: Lindsey Dehaan Dissertation Defense: Morphological Diversification of Fishes in the Wake of Ecological Opportunity: Insights from a Combination of Paleontological and Neontological Data
event_subtitle: Morphological Diversification of Fishes in the Wake of Ecological Opportunity: Insights from a Combination of Paleontological and Neontological Data
description:
Zoom link: https://umich.zoom.us/j/9121902198

The remarkable diversity of body plans observed across species reflects millions of years of morphological change. Environmental disturbances and dispersal into new geographic regions can create ecological opportunities hypothesized to trigger rapid bursts of phenotypic diversification. Perspectives on these evolutionary radiations often stem from patterns of diversity apparent in the fossil record or from reconstructing macroevolutionary dynamics using molecular phylogenies of living species. However, these end-member approaches provide incomplete snapshots of biodiversity. Whereas integrating these two complementary, yet distinct natural history records have the potential to yield more accurate macroevolutionary inferences. In this dissertation, I investigate the morphological diversification of Acanthomorpha (spiny- rayed teleosts), a predominately marine fish radiation comprising more than 25% of all extant vertebrates. I also address methodological challenges associated with integrating data of extant and fossil species into a single phylogenetic framework. Specifically, I use a combination of linear morphometrics and phylogenetic comparative methods to examine how past geological events might have altered the phenotypic evolution of three distantly related acanthomorph lineages. First, I use a combined phylogenetic framework of fossil and extant Tetraodontiformes (pufferfishes and allies) to quantify their mode of evolution and test for a shift in evolutionary rate associated with the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM). Despite their highly distinctive morphologies, I find that tetraodontiforms are characterized by moderately strong morphological and ecological constraints, and that the PETM had no obvious impact on their morphological diversification. Second, I addressed an outstanding obstacle for studies like that of tetraodontiforms: the lack of a combined phylogenetic framework which subsequently limits the inclusion of fossil data in phenotypic inferences. I use simulations to evaluate alternative methods of incorporating fossil taxa into molecular phylogenies in the absence of a formally inferred tree that includes extinct tips. I demonstrate that methods commonly applied in the literature produce the most misleading inferences, whereas estimating branch length durations for fossil tips using continuous trait data provides the most reliable results. When applying these methods to Carangaria (flatfishes, jack, and allies), I recover evidence of a rapid burst of morphological diversification following the end-Cretaceous mass extinction, a pattern that is obscured when extant only taxa are considered. Third and finally, I investigate whether cross-continental dispersal influences rates of phenotypic evolution in spiny eels (Mastacembelidae). Following their origin in Asia, spiny eels underwent a single dispersal event into Africa. I find that African taxa exhibit elevated rates of morphological diversification relative to their Asian counterparts. Surprisingly, this pattern was not driven by the species flock endemic to Lake Tanganyika, suggesting that the macroevolutionary dynamics characteristic of colonizing insular environments (e.g., islands and freshwater lakes) may also emerge at continental scales. Together, this work demonstrates that multiple factors likely led to the remarkable anatomical diversity of Acanthomorpha. These case studies on individual clades also provide a framework for conducting similar work at the scale of acanthomorphs as a whole. More generally, this dissertation highlights the importance of incorporating fossil information into macroevolutionary inferences and the methodological challenges that remain.

event_title: Bookworm #97 - Author Conversation with Anne Ruggles Gere, "Agents of Survivance: Indigenous Women Teachers in the Boarding School Era"
combined_title: Bookworm #97 - Author Conversation with Anne Ruggles Gere, "Agents of Survivance: Indigenous Women Teachers in the Boarding School Era"
description:
In her book, "Agents of Survivance: Indigenous Women Teachers in the Boarding School Era," Anne Ruggles Gere complicates and enriches established accounts of the Indian boarding school era and what preceded it by looking closely at the largely ignored Indigenous women teachers in these schools.

Focusing on Sarah Winnemucca, S. Alice Callahan, Angel DeCora, and Ella Deloria, Gere shows how these and many other Indian women teachers subversively resisted assimilation with tribal presence, relationality, connection to land, rejection of victimhood, and maintenance of cultural traditions, art, and languages. Their vulnerable positions in schools directed by Euro-Americans necessitated that their contributions be subversive, nearly invisible. Despite this, they developed policies and practices that were passed to Indian students who in turn became teachers of the next generation of Indian students, and many of their innovations inform contemporary movements toward sovereignty for Indian education.

This episode is sponsored by the Alumni Association of the University of Michigan Lifelong Learning program and is in recognition of Native American History Month.

combined_title: Morgan DeSantis Seminar
description: Cytoplasmic dynein-1 (dynein) facilitates the microtubule-based retrograde trafficking of all cellular cargo in most eukaryotes. To become active, dynein binds dynactin and one of many cargo-specific adaptors to form the active transport complex. Despite having similar structures, active transport complexes assembled with different adaptors move with different properties. The molecular features in adaptors that underlie the differences in activity is unknown. To explore how adaptors differentially activate dynein, we engineered a library of synthetic adaptors and characterized their ability to activate dynein using in vitro reconstitution and cell-based trafficking assays. We found that the apparent motility of dynein is highly plastic and tunable by the adaptor sequence and that it is possible to engineer adaptors that outperform endogenous adaptors’ ability to generate highly motile active transport complexes, both in vitro and in cells. By performing structure-function analyses with hyperactive, synthetic adaptors, we discovered that increased random coil at key positions in an adaptor sequence increases the likelihood that dynein-dynactin-adaptor complexes that assemble will be motile. Our work supports a model where increased adaptor flexibility facilitates a type of kinetic proofreading that specifically destabilizes improperly assembled and inactive dynein-dynactin-adaptor complexes. These findings provide insight into how dynein motility is modulated to meet the unique trafficking requirements of all cellular cargo.

event_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
combined_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism: Nicola Barham, Curator
description:
The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told.

*Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. He has been a Lecturer at Stamps School of Art & Design since the Fall of 2022. His work is exhibited widely nationally and he is a recipient of the VSC Fellowship at Vermont Studio Center. He has been awarded numerous artist residencies including Anderson Ranch Arts Center, I-Park, KHN Center for the Arts, Prairie Ronde, Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program, and Rockland Woods. event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

event_title: Foraging Household, Community and Cultural Identity Through Food: Comparing Viru (ca. 200 BCE-800 CE) Foodways at Domestic Structures in Puerto Malabrigo, Chicama Valley, Peru, Across Space and Time
combined_title: Foraging Household, Community and Cultural Identity Through Food: Comparing Viru (ca. 200 BCE-800 CE) Foodways at Domestic Structures in Puerto Malabrigo, Chicama Valley, Peru, Across Space and Time: Chloe Twu PhD Student, University of Michigan Department of Anthropology
event_subtitle: Chloe Twu PhD Student, University of Michigan Department of Anthropology
description: Households occupied by the Viru (ca. 200 BCE-800 CE), a key group in the emergence of statehood during the Early Intermediate Period (EIP) Andes, offer a glimpse into food’s role in the construction of group identity, society, and state expansion on the north coast of Peru. The Viru expanded north from their capital, in the Viru Valley, during the first century CE, constructing outposts in the Moche and Chicama valleys. The northernmost Viru site to date was identified in 2023 at Las Pampas, Puerto Malabrigo by Proyecto de Investigación Arqueológica de Puerto Malabrigo (PIAPM), co-directed by Peruvian archaeologist Aleksalia Isla Alayo and UCSD PhD candidate Arianna Garvin Suero. Sediment samples extracted from floors, above-floor fill, and features within floors and fill were collected and analyzed for organic remains, sorted, identified, and catalogued using macrobotanical techniques. This presentation investigates plant food remains found in samples from floors in two structures: areas 5 and 6. Chloe will discuss the results of her undergraduate honors thesis, encompassing spatial analysis between the households, comparing densities and frequencies of select crop, wild, and highland food taxa as connected to household and community-level identity formation, as well as temporal analysis between two distinct construction phases in each household and the implications for change in larger Viru cultural identity. Integrating these results with archaeobotanical studies from the Viru capital, this presentation will demonstrate the importance of food studies in representing how social changes within the Viru state reflect onto domestic settings.

combined_title: NERS Colloquium: Spectroscopy for Nuclear Material Characterization, Plasma Science: Alexander Bataller, North Carolina State University, Department of Nuclear Engineering
event_subtitle: Alexander Bataller, North Carolina State University, Department of Nuclear Engineering
description:
Abstract:
How do you measure what is happening inside liquids that are red-hot, highly reactive, and embedded in intense radiation fields while serving as coolants in advanced nuclear reactors? Over the past six years, my research group has been addressing this challenge by using light, through optical and plasma-based spectroscopy, to study molten salts and liquid metals relevant to advanced reactors, pyroprocessing, and safeguards. In this talk, I will give a big-picture overview of our work, from capturing the chaotic dance of microspheres, to witnessing the life and death of liberated electrons, to blowing plasma bubbles in liquids for applications in advanced nuclear systems. Together, these efforts show how optical access to high-temperature reactor liquids can reduce uncertainty in modeling, enable new sensing capabilities, and support the deployment of next-generation nuclear energy systems.

 
Bio:
Alexander Bataller is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Nuclear Engineering at North Carolina State University. His research focuses on applying optical and plasma-based spectroscopy to the characterization, fundamental science, and sensing of high-temperature liquids relevant to advanced nuclear systems, including molten salt reactors, pyroprocessing, and liquid metal technologies. His group develops non-intrusive diagnostics to measure thermophysical properties, probe ultrafast chemical processes in extreme environments, and enable real-time monitoring for reactor operation and safeguards. Dr. Bataller’s work spans benchtop experiments to loopintegrated demonstrations and is supported by DOE Nuclear Energy programs in collaboration with national laboratories and industry partners.

The NERS Colloquia Series invites leading researchers, industry experts, and thought leaders from across the nuclear engineering and radiological sciences community to share their insights with students, faculty, and guests. Covering a wide range of topics—from cutting-edge research and emerging technologies to policy, education, and professional development—the weekly talks offer an opportunity to explore current issues and innovations shaping the future of the field.

As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow.

The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

event_title: The Franchise Gap: Fissuring, Job Quality, and Labor Standards Compliance
combined_title: The Franchise Gap: Fissuring, Job Quality, and Labor Standards Compliance: Daniel Schneider, Harvard Kennedy School
description: Work has increasingly re-organized and fissured: the breakdown of traditional employment relations has pushed lower-income workers into lower-income firms (Weil, 2014), including through sub-contracting, outsourcing, and franchising. A growing empirical literature links such arrangements to declines in job quality along several dimensions, with studies of domestic outsourcing documenting sizable wage penalties (Dube and Kaplan 2010; Goldschmidt and Schmieder 2017) and generally elevated employment instability (Aeppli 2025). We contribute to the literature on fissuring and job quality by examining the case of franchising, which has gone relatively little examined due to limits of existing data. We take on this question by deploying two sources of novel linked data in the US context. First, we use a national individual-level sample of thousands of hourly workers employed at dozens of fast food firms surveyed between 2019 and 2025 collected by The Shift Project. These data provide both unusually detailed direct worker reports of job quality and the capacity to link responses at the firm level to organizational attributes. We make use of this capacity for linkage by leveraging a second source of novel data, legally required annual Franchise Disclosure Documents (FDDs), which report, by state and year, the number of company-owned and franchised outlets as well as detailed contractual provisions that aim to standardize production. We scraped state-firm-year level counts of franchised and company-owned establishments for major fast-food chains for the years 2019 to 2024. We show that workers in franchised fast-food restaurants make, on average, $1.7\hr less than workers in non-franchised fast-food restaurants, and have, on average, a 40-50 p.p. lower rate of access to paid sick leave and a stable schedule. In an overall job quality index, including dimensions such as wages, quality of hours worked, scheduling, fringe benefits, and work-life balance, franchisee companies have, on average, a score that is 3/4 of a standard deviation lower than that of non-franchise companies. Using the staggered implementation of Paid Sick Leave policies across 11 states, we show that these policies reduced the gap in access to PSL by 26 percentage points. Despite the substantial effect of the law’s introduction in reducing the gap, we also document rampant non-compliance with these laws: over 60% of workers in PSL jurisdictions in franchised establishments have their right to paid sick leave violated.

event_title: CSEAS Friday Lecture Series | Between the Nitu and New Faiths: Understanding Local Religious Worlds and the Appeal of Conversion in Early Modern Eastern Indonesia
combined_title: CSEAS Friday Lecture Series | Between the Nitu and New Faiths: Understanding Local Religious Worlds and the Appeal of Conversion in Early Modern Eastern Indonesia: Benjamin Moseley, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa
event_subtitle: Benjamin Moseley, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa
description:
Please note: This lecture will be held virtually on Zoom. Registration is required. Once you've registered, joining information will be sent to your email. Register for the Zoom webinar at: https://myumi.ch/nVJ7b

Between the late fifteenth and early seventeenth centuries, the islands of Southeast Asia’s eastern archipelago—particularly those within Indonesia’s present-day provinces of Maluku, North Maluku, and East Nusa Tenggara—became the site of overlapping and competitive processes of Islamization and Christianization. The peoples of the region actively interpreted, adapted, and integrated these faiths within existing cultural, political, and spiritual frameworks. Understanding these encounters, however, requires reconstructing the religious worlds of communities that left few written records of their own. Scholars must therefore critically examine missionary and colonial accounts alongside nineteenth- and twentieth-century ethnographies, remaining attentive to observers’ biases and the historical changes separating these sources. Focusing on Ambon, North Maluku, and Flores, this talk explores how to uncover earlier understandings of relations between humans and spirits (nitu), ritual obligations, and cosmological dualism. It also considers how these understandings shaped the appeal of Islam and Christianity and the meanings of conversion, as people negotiated new teachings and practices alongside established beliefs and obligations.

BENJAMIN L. MOSELEY earned his PhD. in history from the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa in Spring 2026. His dissertation examined patterns of religious conversion and the relationships among Christianity, Islam, and local belief systems in early modern eastern Indonesia.

event_title: AIM Seminar:  Quantum Gibbs Sampling: Mixing, Algorithm Design, and Measurement
combined_title: AIM Seminar:  Quantum Gibbs Sampling: Mixing, Algorithm Design, and Measurement: Hongrui Chen (Mathematics, Stanford)
description:
Abstract:  Quantum Gibbs states describe the thermal equilibrium of quantum many-body systems and underlie many central questions in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry. Preparing these states is a natural task for quantum computers, and a promising approach is quantum Gibbs sampling, which runs a quantum analogue of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) whose stationary state is the Gibbs state. In this talk, I will first introduce the basic ideas of quantum Gibbs sampling, drawing analogies with classical MCMC along the way, and then discuss three questions about these algorithms.

First, how fast do they converge? For one-dimensional spin chains at any temperature, we show that a standard detailed-balanced quantum Gibbs sampler mixes in polylogarithmic time, using a spectral analysis that goes beyond the spectral gap.

Second, can they be made simple? We construct samplers based on weakly coupling the system to a small bath, which avoids the heavy machinery of exact samplers. We show that a detailed-balance structure, together with randomized interaction times, removes the bias induced by the bath.

Third, how do we read out the result? Instead of destroying the state at each measurement, we design non-destructive measurements that preserve, or nearly preserve, the Gibbs state, reducing the cost per sample from the full mixing time to the autocorrelation time.

Contact:  Zhiyan Ding

description: Recent years have seen a dramatic expansion in ideas regarding the nature of dark matter, extending beyond the WIMP paradigm. Many of these theories predict minuscule couplings between light (sub-GeV mass) dark matter and the Standard Model, which direct detection experiments can search for. In this talk we will begin by reviewing the status of current electron-based experiments which are achieving extraordinary sensitivity to theoretically well-motivated freeze-in dark matter models. event_title: Student Algebraic Geometry: Moduli of Cubic Surfaces and Complex Hyperbolic Geometry
combined_title: Student Algebraic Geometry: Moduli of Cubic Surfaces and Complex Hyperbolic Geometry: Aaron Kim
description: We discuss the theorem of Allcock-Carlson-Toledo identifying the moduli space of stable complex cubic surfaces with B^4/Γ, where B^4 is the complex hyperbolic 4-ball and Γ is an explicit arithmetic lattice in PU(4,1) generated by complex reflections of order six (called “hexflections”). Although the usual period map for cubic surfaces is constant, a construction following ideas going back to Picard produces a nontrivial period map using associated cyclic cubic threefolds. We explain this construction and use Picard-Lefschetz theory to relate nodal degenerations to the mirrors of hexflections. In particular, removing the images of these mirrors from the ball quotient gives the moduli space of smooth cubic surfaces. We conclude with more examples of moduli spaces admitting similar ball quotient descriptions and briefly discuss recent work on their geometry and topology.

combined_title: Weak Separation on the Annulus: Beinuo Guo (University of Michigan)
description:
Weak separation is a combinatorial relation on subsets of cyclically ordered points, generalizing the notion of noncrossing diagonals. Oh, Postnikov, and Speyer established a correspondence between maximal weakly separated collections and reduced plabic graphs on a disk, proving that these collections are pure and connected by mutations.

In this talk, we investigate an analogue of weak separation on an annulus by passing to its universal cover. We study the resulting simplicial complexes, proving purity and describing their topological properties in several special cases. We then introduce periodic plabic graphs and establish a move-connectivity theorem for reduced graphs with a fixed lifted strand permutation, adapting techniques involving triple diagrams. We will discuss how these results contribute toward extending the correspondence of Oh, Postnikov, and Speyer to the annulus.

This is joint work with Iz Chen, Jan Fedyszyn, Reyna Li, and Rosa Paten, mentored by Pasha Pylyavskyy.

combined_title: Smith Lecture: Basil Tikoff: The interaction of magmatism and tectonism in magmatic arcs
event_subtitle: The interaction of magmatism and tectonism in magmatic arcs
description: Magmatic arcs result from subduction along a convergent plate boundary.  The relative movement of the plates is rarely orthogonal and there is often concurrent deformation in the back-arc region.  Consequently, there is generally an interplay between tectonism and magmatism in magmatic arcs.   This talk discusses a series of magmatic arcs that I have studied in my career, including the Cretaceous Sierra Nevada magmatic arc in California, the active magmatic arc in El Salvador and Guatemala, and the Laguna de Maule volcanic field in the active Andean arc in Chile.  The short summary is that granite magmas appear to need strike-slip faults to rise through the crust, deformation follows the magmatism in almost all cases, the granitic plutons are incrementally emplaced, and the deformation in the back-arc has a major impact on the magmatic arc.

event_title: Beyond Problem Solving: AI for Problem Generation, Abstraction and Generalization
combined_title: Beyond Problem Solving: AI for Problem Generation, Abstraction and Generalization: Gabriel Poesia
description:
AI has made remarkable progress in solving well-defined mathematical problems, advancing in just a few years from grade-school exercises to helping settle problems at the research frontier. In this talk, I'll present recent and ongoing work from my new lab at U-M CSE on AI systems for tasks beyond problem solving, with applications to both formal mathematics and software. I'll first present The Token Games, an evaluation framework in which AI models challenge each other with puzzles they generate, inspired by Renaissance-era mathematical duels. We find that scores from The Token Games strongly correlate with performance on existing reasoning benchmarks, while being cheaper to obtain and easier to extend, since it's problem pool is not fixed. However, while useful for evaluation, the problems generated in these duels are largely "uninteresting" to humans. In another recent work, we compared human and LLM judgments of problem interestingness, finding that while some models agree substantially with humans on which problems are interesting, they often fail to identify why humans find them interesting. Finally, I'll briefly discuss preliminary work on learning useful, reusable abstractions from formal proofs, including generalizing theorems, synthesizing proof tactics, and discovering new definitions through symbolic program compression.

Bio: Gabriel Poesia is a new Assistant Professor of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. His research lies at the intersection of formal reasoning and AI, grounded in applications in program verification and formal mathematics. combined_title: “Small Dance Party” – MFA Thesis Dance Concert by Kei Tsuruharatani: A Meditative Exploration of Queer Movement and Stillness
event_subtitle: A Meditative Exploration of Queer Movement and Stillness
description:
The University of Michigan School of Music, Theatre & Dance presents *Small Dance Party* by Master of Fine Arts in Dance candidate Kei Tsuruharatani. This event is an immersive performance installation that shifts the focus of dance from exterior virtuosity to interior listening. An improvisational score will be performed at 6:45 pm and 7:45 pm. Guests are invited to come and go whenever during those two hours.

*Small Dance Party* investigates the intersection of trans/queer studies and dance studies by centering softness, attunement, and the ordinary as radical sites of inquiry. While acknowledging the highly virtuosic performances often found in queer communities, this project offers an alternative: a queer dance space that values quiet listening to the body and the environment. By framing dance as an art of attention in space and time, the installation turns toward the mundane movements of everyday life. Outside the bounds of traditional entertainment, dance becomes a critical, living lens to examine transness – revealing the internal movement that happens while transitioning.

During the event, with music composition by Molly Jones, participants and observers are invited into a shared meditative space. The installation asks attendees to yield control: rather than commanding the body, participants are invited to listen to what the body has to say. By engaging with the rhythm of the internal body, the sway of gravity, and the expansion of breath, *Small Dance Party* creates a deeply somatic environment for queering body, movement, and stillness.

This project is being held in partial fulfillment of the Master of Fine Arts in Dance degree requirements. It was made possible by support from the Department of Dance, William Braddan McClellan, Jr. Fund in Dance, Excel Lab & Career Center, SMTD Wellness Program, Eisenberg Family Depression Center, and the Arts Initiative at the University of Michigan.

description:
Jack Tucker is hilariously awful, and that’s precisely the point.

The Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show is the misguided brainchild of Zach Zucker, a performer who is celebrated for blending virtuosic clowning with razor-sharp satire. His character Jack Tucker is a well-respected journeyman and bonafide legend on the Upstate New York regional comedy scene, a catastrophically overconfident stand-up comedian whose hacky punchlines, misplaced swagger, and desperate need to be adored convince him that he’s going to make it big any day now.

As his jokes collapse and his bravado frays, the show exposes the fragile ego beneath the spotlight and the quiet terror behind the mic. Equal parts parody, performance art, and masterclass in comedic tension, Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show walks a thrilling line, with Zach Zucker’s physical control and improvisational daring bringing both discipline and danger to the chaos.

Zucker, whose clown lineage dates to the famous École Philippe Gaulier in France, the training ground for actors such as Sacha Baron Cohen, Helena Bonham Carter, Emma Thompson, and many others, is a cult favorite on the international comedy circuit, known for his always sold-out Stamptown Comedy and a forthcoming Netflix special.

Recommended for mature audiences.

combined_title: Steve Poltz: Presented by The Ark
description:
New music!

A dude named Steve Poltz (me) in East Nashville wakes up one morning and gets a call from another dude in East Nashville named Dex Green. Dex says, “Hey man, you live so close. You oughta come over and make some music. Maybe we’ll document it — who knows, maybe it’s a record.”

Capturing me in a studio is like convincing a whirling dervish to stop spinning long enough to sign a bill into law. It’s chaos, caffeine, and accidental poetry — art colliding with microphones and commerce in a glorious mess. That’s how JoyRide happened. No seatbelts, no helmets. Just unsaturated, unadulterated art. Real humans making real noise in real time.

JoyRide is my 14th solo album (not counting the Rugburns records, live things, and bootlegs floating around). I tour nonstop, so I usually have to be tricked into a studio under the guise of “just one song.”

The record opens with “If It Bleeds It Leads” — my kinda classic mischief:

“I can never watch the news with you because you yell back — you scream like they can hear you in the television set.”

Then comes “Petrichor,” inspired by the beautiful smell after it rains. (I later discovered Phish has one too, but mine’s the barefoot cousin at brunch.)

“At It Again” follows, a cosmic co-write with my brother-from-another-meerkat Jim Lauderdale, featuring Bryan Owings and Chris Donohue (Emmylou Harris’s rhythm section).

The title track “JoyRide” feels like a warm hug after a long road trip:

“Free hugs, no shrugs, wrong drugs, bedbugs. Smiles, laughter, for here ever after.”

Side one ends with “The Son Of God.” 
A nutso magutso  track of a conversation I  may or may not have had with Jesus.“ I get to play both parts. Myself AND Jesus.
“The son of God contacted me about buying some Funk and Wagnalls encyclopedias. I said hello who’s this?”
“It’s Jesus”
“Jesus who?”
“Jesus H. Christ. God’s son.”
“How’d you get my number?”
“I have everyone’s number.”
“Even Liberace?”
“He’s on dead people's speed dial.”

I will probably get crucified for this song, but hopefully it will be an AI video made by an angry man living in his mom’s basement. 

Side two kicks off with “Love a Little Bigger” — a rowdy co-write with Vince Herman of Leftover Salmon. It opens with:

“Jacob took a hammer and he went up a hill, built a nice house for his best friend Bill…”
and ends with a singalong reminder to forgive faster and swim more often.

“Fixin’ Up” (track seven) is my secret favorite — like a quarter from the Tooth Fairy you gotta dig around for.
“New Tattoo” follows — about a dude who got his lover’s face inked on his own face. (Bad plan, good song.)
“Brand New Liver” imagines swapping out your old one like a water pump instead of quitting drinking.
And then comes the closer: “Hairlift.”

That one has my favorite line I’ve ever written:

“I used to play ping pong with my old friend Mao Zedong. I thought he told me I was well hung, but he was speaking in the mother tongue.”

description:
From September 2025 through December 2026, Stamps Gallery is partnering in a curatorial collaboration with two Southeast Michigan-based, artist-run project spaces led by Stamps alumni: C.Y.N.K. Studios, directed by Sally Clegg (Lecturer III and Student Exhibition Coordinator, MFA ’20) and Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20); and Sometimes Space, directed by Nathan Byrne (Lecturer I, MFA ’21). For this project, Byrne, Clegg, and Narula have been commissioned to reimagine the pillars on Division Street that flank the gallery. Phase 2 (January 12 - August 12) artists: Sally Clegg (MFA ’20) and Kim Karlsrud (MFA ’20)

Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. He has been a Lecturer at Stamps School of Art & Design since the Fall of 2022. His work is exhibited widely nationally and he is a recipient of the VSC Fellowship at Vermont Studio Center. He has been awarded numerous artist residencies including Anderson Ranch Arts Center, I-Park, KHN Center for the Arts, Prairie Ronde, Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program, and Rockland Woods. event_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
combined_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism: Nicola Barham, Curator
description:
The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told.

*Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

event_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
combined_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show: Performed by Zach Zucker
description:
Jack Tucker is hilariously awful, and that’s precisely the point.

The Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show is the misguided brainchild of Zach Zucker, a performer who is celebrated for blending virtuosic clowning with razor-sharp satire. His character Jack Tucker is a well-respected journeyman and bonafide legend on the Upstate New York regional comedy scene, a catastrophically overconfident stand-up comedian whose hacky punchlines, misplaced swagger, and desperate need to be adored convince him that he’s going to make it big any day now.

As his jokes collapse and his bravado frays, the show exposes the fragile ego beneath the spotlight and the quiet terror behind the mic. Equal parts parody, performance art, and masterclass in comedic tension, Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show walks a thrilling line, with Zach Zucker’s physical control and improvisational daring bringing both discipline and danger to the chaos.

Zucker, whose clown lineage dates to the famous École Philippe Gaulier in France, the training ground for actors such as Sacha Baron Cohen, Helena Bonham Carter, Emma Thompson, and many others, is a cult favorite on the international comedy circuit, known for his always sold-out Stamptown Comedy and a forthcoming Netflix special.

Recommended for mature audiences.

combined_title: Telegraph Quartet: Music by George Rochberg, Franz Joseph Haydn, and Osvaldo Golijov
event_subtitle: Music by George Rochberg, Franz Joseph Haydn, and Osvaldo Golijov
description:
Acclaimed Telegraph Quartet, now in residency at the School of Music, Theatre & Dance, performs a recital. The program highlights music shaped by the idea of revisitation – it includes George Rochberg’s String Quintet (performed with cellist Norman Fischer); Franz Joseph Haydn’s String Quartet Op. 76, No. 2 “Quinten”; and Osvaldo Golijov’s *Ever Yours*, a string octet performed with Fischer, violist Matt Albert, and violinists River Sawchyn and Aidan Krieger. Composed in different eras, these works by Rochberg, Haydn, and Golijov each center on the idea of returning to something: musical ideas embraced before or the meanings behind emotions that influence the composers’ work.

Initially known for his use of serialism – an approach to composing that focuses on creating sequences using pitches, rhythms, dynamics, or other musical elements – Rochberg turned to writing music with a more melodic style after the death of his son in 1964. Rochberg claimed he couldn’t fully express his grief in music that used serialism’s pattern-focused approach. His 1982 String Quintet reflects Rochberg returns to the familiarity of more traditional melodic expression, and though critics thought it was a creative regression, the music still conveys what Rochberg viewed as an expanded emotional range.

Haydn’s String Quartet Op. 76, No. 2 “Quinten” bucked the composer’s trend of composing grand, bright, vibrant music and is instead written almost entirely in D minor, which is often described as the saddest and most melancholy of all keys. The piece is nicknamed “Quinten,” meaning fifths, because of Haydn’s frequent use of this foundational interval between notes. Composed when he was in his 60s, after a lifetime of writing some of the most sophisticated, expressive, and innovative works of his time, this quartet showcases Haydn’s ability to create impressive work even with the most basic elements.

After being asked to compose an octet for the Amsterdam String Quartet Biennale, Osvaldo Golijov re-read letters Vincent Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo. The small but consistent detail of Van Gogh’s letters closing with “ever yours” prompted Golijov to reflect on the enduring bonds between himself, the St. Lawrence Quartet, and their late first violinist, co-founder, and force of nature, Geoff Nuttall, to whom the octet is dedicated. At the time, Nuttall was battling pancreatic cancer, which would ultimately take his life. In thinking about Nuttall, Golijov came to consider the idea of Van Gogh’s “ever yours” mentality and how attention can connect to love. Through that attention-minded lens, Golijov saw a bond between Nuttall, Van Gogh, and Haydn, a composer of whom Nuttall was especially fond, ultimately connecting the three across time and creative spaces. 

The Telegraph Quartet was truly honored to work with Nuttall, the St. Lawrence Quartet, and Golijov in the actual formation of the work. Golijov composed the music almost before the ensemble’s very ears, using the instrumentation of the octet and aesthetic feedback from the Telegraph’s players to stimulate his own creative process. The work was dedicated to Nuttall, who, along with the St. Lawrence and Telegraph Quartets, premiered the work at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music.

ABOUT TELEGRAPH QUARTET
Erin Chin & Joseph Maile, violins
Pei-Ling Lin, viola
Jeremiah Shaw, cello

The TELEGRAPH QUARTET formed in 2013 with an equal passion for standard and contemporary chamber music repertoire. Described by the *San Francisco Chronicle* as “…an incredibly valuable addition to the cultural landscape” and “powerfully adept… with a combination of brilliance and subtlety,” the Telegraph Quartet was awarded the prestigious 2016 Walter W. Naumburg Chamber Music Award and the Grand Prize at the 2014 Fischoff Chamber Music Competition. The quartet is currently the quartet-in-residence at the University of Michigan.

The quartet has performed in New York City’s Carnegie Hall and Lincoln Center, San Francisco’s Herbst Theatre, the San Francisco Conservatory of Music’s *Chamber Masters Series*, and at festivals including the Chautauqua Institute, Kneisel Hall Chamber Music Festival, and the Emilia Romagna Festival. They have collaborated with pianists Leon Fleisher and Simone Dinnerstein; cellists Norman Fischer and Bonnie Hampton; violinist Ian Swensen; and the St. Lawrence Quartet and Henschel Quartett. A fervent champion of 20th- and 21st-century repertoire, the Telegraph Quartet has premiered works by Osvaldo Golijov, John Harbison, Robert Sirota, and Richard Festinger.

In 2023, the Telegraph Quartet released *20th Century Vantage Points: Divergent Paths*, the first in a trilogy of recordings on Azica Records exploring the string quartets of the first half of the 20th century – an era of music that the group has felt especially called to perform since its formation. *Divergent Paths* features two works that (to the best of the quartet’s knowledge) have never been recorded on the same album before: Maurice Ravel’s String Quartet in F Major and Arnold Schoenberg’s String Quartet no. 1 in D minor, op. 7. The quartet’s new album, *20th Century Vantage Points: Edge of the Storm* is out now on Azica Records.

description: Set against the streets of New York City, West Side Story is a timeless tale of love, rivalry, and the search for belonging. With a book by Arthur Laurents, music by Leonard Bernstein, and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, this iconic musical brings Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet to life. When Tony, a former member of the Jets, falls deeply in love with Maria, the sister of the leader of the rival Sharks, their romance sparks a chain of events that threatens to tear their divided community apart. As the Jets and Sharks fight for control of the neighborhood, Tony and Maria dream of a world where they can build a life together beyond the boundaries that separate them. Filled with unforgettable music, breathtaking dance, and moments of joy and heartbreak, West Side Story explores the power of love in the face of hatred, the complexities of identity and belonging, and the consequences of division.

In 1895, playwright and poet Oscar Wilde sued the Marquess of Queensberry for criminal libel after the Marquess called him a “posing sodomite.” This lawsuit backfired on Wilde, resulting in two additional trials to determine whether Wilde was guilty of “gross indecency with male persons.” 

Playwright Moisés Kaufman, the Tony- and Emmy-nominated playwright behind *The Laramie Project*, uses trial transcripts, personal correspondence, interviews, and other source materials to tell the story of the downfall of the great man of letters whose artistic genius has long been overshadowed by the scandal surrounding his imprisonment.

The show follows the fictional town of Grover’s Corners, New Hampshire, starting in 1901, full of ordinary people going about their daily lives. In the context of the show, a copy of the play was to go in a time capsule, so, as the Stage Manager puts it, “the people a thousand years from now’ll know a few simple facts about us,” “the way we were: in our growing up and in our marrying and in our living and in our dying.” I think you’ll find that their ordinary lives aren’t so detached from ours.

description:
Over the last thirty-five years, Canadian Music Hall of Fame inductee Steven Page has established himself as one of the most recognizable and enduring voices in music. The release of his latest album, Excelsior, shows that he has no plans of slowing down anytime soon. 

As a co-founder, vocalist and songwriter for Barenaked Ladies, Steven sang and wrote classics like “Brian Wilson,” “If I Had A Million Dollars,” “What A Good Boy,” “It’s All Been Done” and many more. With the band, he sold over 15 Million albums and scored multiple Junos, Billboard Music Awards, SOCAN awards, Gemini Awards and two Grammy nominations. After leaving the band in 2009, Steven embarked on a solo career that has produced five solo albums, including 2022’s Excelsior, and has seen him tour worldwide, from folk festivals to cabarets and theatres, all the way to packed arenas on a string of dates opening for rock legends The Who.
​
Steven performs in many configurations, but, since 2016, has been playing most often with his pals in The Steven Page Trio, Craig Northey of Vancouver legends Odds on guitar, and Kevin Fox on cello. With SP3, Steven has performed arrangements of some of his best-loved songs from his long career with symphony orchestras including the Vancouver and Winnipeg Symphony Orchestras. 

Steven is a frequent collaborator with Toronto’s eclectic Art of Time Ensemble, is a member of power-pop quartet, The Trans-Canada Highwaymen, has a Stratford commissioned musical in the works, and continues to work in film, television and other media. The Governor-General’s Performing Arts Awards asked Steven to write a song as a surprise tribute to his friend, Ryan Reynolds, and the result was “Canada Loves You Back,” a song as poignant, humorous and Canadian as the actor it honors.

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

combined_title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them: Exhibit
description:
Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking.

While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last.

Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

description:
Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

event_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
combined_title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism: Nicola Barham, Curator
description:
The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told.

*Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

combined_title: The Tree of Eternity: Interactive arttech exhibit
description:
The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. 

The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure.

Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree.

As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow.

The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

combined_title: Black Washtenaw County and the Civil War: Motorcoach and Walking Tour: The African American Cultural and Historical Museum of Washtenaw County
event_subtitle: The African American Cultural and Historical Museum of Washtenaw County
description:
Visit the sites connected to Black Civil War veterans who called Washtenaw County home. Historians Deborah Meadows and Matthew Siegfried will lead visitors on a motorcoach and walking journey through Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti including historic Black neighborhoods, Depot Town, and Highland Cemetery, the final resting place of at least 19 Black Civil War soldiers.

This tour is presented in conjunction with the Frankel Detroit Observatory’s exhibit, “Fill the Ranks”: The Civil War and the University of Michigan, and is offered in partnership with the African American Cultural and Historical Museum of Washtenaw County.

Free and open to the public. Limited availability; registration required.

Tour will depart from and return to intersection of Maynard and E. Jefferson Streets (near the Cube). Includes driving and walking portions, including at least one hour of walking and standing. Tour will be rescheduled only in the event of severe weather. Motorcoach transportation provided by Golden Limousine. Please indicate accessibility needs in registration.

Matthew Siegfried is a historian, writer and researcher. He has collaborated with schools, universities, libraries, and the African American Cultural and Historical Museum of Washtenaw County. He has done extensive research on Ypsilanti’s historic African American neighborhood and communities, sharing his findings at the South Adams Street @ 1900 website.

Deborah Meadows is lead docent for the African American Cultural and Historical Museum of Washtenaw County.

Founded in 1993, the African American Cultural and Historical Museum of Washtenaw County researches, collects, preserves, and exhibits cultural and historical materials about the life and work of African Americans in Washtenaw County.

This program is presented with support from the University of Michigan’s U.S. at 250 initiative and the Inclusive History Project.
